#7497. How the BMW Group governs hundreds of agents across thousands of developers

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2088 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Amazon ↗ Open Full Page

How the BMW Group governs hundreds of agents across thousands of developers

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2088 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When hundreds of agents serve thousands of developers, enterprise governance can’t be an afterthought.
  • Industry observers note that at the BMW Group’s R&D, more than 12,500 developers work on approximately 500 million lines of vehicle software code.
  • While research, frameworks, and guidelines now facilitate building agents, industrializing and operating high-quality agents in an efficient, scalable manner remains a significant challenge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When hundreds of agents serve thousands of developers, enterprise governance can’t be an afterthought.

Industry observers note that at the BMW Group’s R&D, more than 12,500 developers work on approximately 500 million lines of vehicle software code. This software is augmented by the BMW Connected Vehicle backend, a cloud-based system of more than 1,300 microservices providing digital services for 24 million vehicles in the field. In regulated industry, the bar for (software) quality, stability, and governance compliance is exceptionally high.

While research, frameworks, and guidelines now facilitate building agents, industrializing and operating high-quality agents in an efficient, scalable manner remains a significant challenge.

Scaling agentic AI across a large organization cannot be achieved by isolated teams. It requires collective effort, locally driven experimentation, and active knowledge sharing across the enterprise. This creates a fundamental governance dichotomy: Development teams need the freedom to innovate rapidly, while the enterprise must enforce standards for safety, security, composability, and cost-efficiency. Without that balance, organizations risk a fragmented landscape of AI islands and costly duplicate work. This presents a real challenge given hundreds of globally distributed teams building agents across the BMW Group.

In this post, we detail the practices and patterns that support BMW’s R&D teams in building, governing and operating agents at scale without sacrificing speed, quality or compliance.

Our premise is straightforward: build agents that can cooperate from the start. This requires an architecture that makes diversity composable, governable, and automatable, without requiring a single framework or toolchain.

It has been revealed that central to this architecture is the agent harness, a runtime layer wrapped around a large language model (LLM). It provides the execution loop, tool dispatch, memory management, and observability hooks for autonomous operation.

Just as the AWS Well-Architected Framework standardized cloud infrastructure design, agentic systems need equivalent patterns, reusable blueprints encoding governance, composability, and operational best practices from the start.

We organize our solution around five interlocking practices, drawn from hands-on experience building and operating agentic systems at enterprise scale since 2023. Each practice is codified as infrastructure as code (IaC), making adoption repeatable, auditable, and enforceable across teams without blocking DevOps velocity.

In a recent development, governance must be structural from the start and maintained across the full lifecycle. We advocate for three properties of effective agentic governance:.

Framework-agnostic and externalized: Governance rules such as authentication, authorization, rate limiting and content filtering are enforced at the integration layer. This includes a Model Context Protocol (MCP) gateway, a central agent registry and orchestration boundary, rather than within individual agent codebases. This means governance survives framework migrations, model swaps, and team reorganizations.

Recent findings suggest that domain-sensitive and graduated: Not every agent action carries the same risk: drafting documentation, updating customer records, and production database writes demand very different levels of oversight. We implement graduated trust through per-step autonomy levels:.

Assign trust levels per step, not per agent. A single workflow can include steps at all three levels, so teams can start conservatively and incrementally increase autonomy as confidence builds, grounded in measurable evaluation data, not assumptions.

Deterministically enforced: Governance runs as deterministic code outside the agent’s reasoning loop. In practice, this happens mainly in the CI/CD pipeline. Permission checks, policy-as-code rules, and compliance validations gate every deployment there, before an agent reaches production. Because these checks run separately from the agent, neither the agent nor its prompts are in a position to override them. Egress controls (recipient allowlisting, outbound secret scanning) help prevent an agent holding confidential data from disclosing it through an otherwise legitimate call.

Observability in agentic systems goes beyond traditional application monitoring. The real question is no longer whether a service returned an HTTP 200 status, but whether an agent produced a faithful, policy-compliant output, and how this can be demonstrated through observable execution traces. Answering that requires a ground-truth dataset covering common queries and edge cases. This dataset is used for evaluation from day one, so quality is measured against representative and appropriately governed evaluation datasets for evaluation, not synthetic prompts.

In a recent development, this infrastructure cannot be retrofitted and must be part of the initial design. The continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipeline enforces this, so agents lacking instrumentation fail validation before evaluation runs.

We recommend instrumenting three dimensions:.

Sources indicate that for distributed cloud systems, the industry solved the complexity of end-to-end workflows by adopting architectural patterns such as microservices or service meshes. The evolution of agentic systems needs to follow a similar trajectory, moving from monolithic, generalist agents toward multiple collaborating specialized agents.

Industry observers note that teams should define the problem before considering agents’ functionality. Before writing any orchestration logic, they should produce five concrete artifacts:.

This discipline prevents the most common failure modes we observe: agents that take on too many responsibilities accumulate bloated prompts, reducing accuracy and increasing latency.

Once a single agent is well-scoped, it must be designed as a composable building block. Therefore, we define a three-tier composition hierarchy:.

Recent findings suggest that each tier is validated independently in the CI/CD pipeline. Component tests cover tools and skills, interaction tests cover their composition into flows.

These tiers are connected through open standards: MCP and Agent Skills for tool integration, the protocol for agent-to-agent communication, and OpenTelemetry for observability across the resulting interactions.

Figure 1 reveals how the three tiers build on each other, from individual MCP tools at the base to complete flows at the top.

Figure 1: Three-tier system to build composable agents.

In production, even well-scoped agents can break down as real-world usage diverges from what was anticipated at design time: query patterns shift, tool-selection logic struggles, and performance degrades unpredictably.

The right response is to decompose complex agents into multiple specialized ones, each with clearer instructions, simpler tool sets, and more focused reasoning. The benefits are concrete:.

Complexity can be reduced along two axes:.

Critically, since each specialized agent only accesses the data and tools required for its role, this architecture helps to enforce least-privilege by design, a compliance requirement in regulated industries.

Realizing these benefits, however, requires that agents can find and interoperate with each other. To prevent the emergence of AI islands, we maintain a centralized registry of agents, tools, and skills. This registry serves as:.

The shift from managing individual agents to governing an agent fleet requires agent architectures to be codified. Using Infrastructure-as-code frameworks such as Terraform or AWS CloudFormation, teams provision and manage agent infrastructure with the same rigor applied to any production system:.

All three are enforced as pipeline gates, validated before registration, not audited after the fact.

Sources indicate that the adoption model is deliberately bottom-up with central curation. Individual teams build skills and MCP tools to solve their immediate problems. All teams can contribute by sharing their assets through the registry. A central team builds automatic governance checks as part of the CI pipeline to uphold standards. To support development teams and foster shift-left, the central team additionally provides building blocks as governance-as-code modules.

Recent findings suggest that this balance avoids both centrally mandated architectures and unmanaged experimentation. As a result, when upcoming operational concerns arise, teams can extend existing patterns rather than redesign their architectures.

Architectural patterns and governance standards are only effective if they are embedded into the workflows teams use to build and operate agents before and at runtime.

Industry observers note that governance begins before a single line of orchestration logic is written. Teams are provided with reference architecture patterns and examples drawn from the registry. These pre-validated blueprints cover common agent configurations, tool integration patterns, and composition structures, which accelerate development while encoding proven defaults. Before anything reaches production, standardized CI/CD controls enforce these practices. Figure 2 shows the four phases of a reference pipeline, which run in order from left to right.

Figure 2: Reference pattern for a four-phase agent deployment pipeline.

Phase 1 from Figure 2 runs fast, deterministic checks: supply chain security (approved registries only), component and interaction testing, evaluation library references, and observability instrumentation.

Phase 2 runs security and governance checks in parallel. Static analysis scans the code for concerns, and security tests probe the agent in an isolated staging environment. The pipeline also validates egress controls and least-privilege permissions. Two more checks confirm that the agent’s declared autonomy level matches its actual permissions and that its configuration passes the policy-as-code rules. A governance agent accelerates audits by checking the agent against established standards and flagging findings for human review, such as:.

Figure 3: Example governance agent workflow.

In a recent development, this assessment surfaces concrete, actionable measures that teams can apply immediately, rather than abstract recommendations. Figure 3 shows the governance agent’s dashboard for an agent maturity assessment. The governance agent provides evidence and actionable recommendations, while accountable humans own governance decisions. Recommendations require human confirmation before being applied, maintaining a four-eyes principle for accountability. Findings update the agent’s governance status in the registry, while full details are logged separately in a central knowledge base for audit and traceability.

Phase 3 evaluates the agent as a running system: the ground-truth evaluation gate (scores outputs against benchmarks established at design time) and agent performance (latency, token consumption). Figure 4 details the metrics, scoring criteria and the relationships between them.

Figure 4: Overview of evaluation metrics.

In a recent development, phase 4 checks for duplicates before registering the agent, its sub-agents, tools, and skills. The following table highlights the metadata fields stored per agent in the registry.

Table 1: Example agent metadata stored in the registry.

If any step fails or metrics deteriorate, the deployment stops with logs for root cause analysis. If all checks pass, the agent is packaged and deployed as a containerized workload, producing consistent, reproducible deployments. This prevents ungoverned agents from reaching production, automates compliance checks, and keeps the registry accurate.

At runtime, observability has to catch two kinds of drift. Data drift shows up as new or shifting user query patterns, or changes in upstream APIs. Model drift shows as rising error rates or falling tool-selection accuracy. When a customer flags a response, that also triggers an investigation. Alerts for drift, distribution shifts, declining evaluation scores, or direct customer flags prompt a staged response. These events are logged and forwarded to human review. Additionally, teams can run the governance agent continuously to flag drift and operational issues for the responsible team to investigate.

Building and operating agents at scale is an engineering discipline, not an experimentation exercise.

Industry observers note that effective governance must be structural from the start, externalized, domain-sensitive, and deterministically enforced. We introduced a three-tier composition hierarchy (MCP tools, skills, and flows) as the architectural foundation for reusable, composable, and interoperable agents, decomposed into specialized agents to contain complexity and scope. We showed how verification and evaluation in every CI/CD run make quality assurance part of everyday development, and how defining agent infrastructure as code lets teams apply the same governance rules to every agent in the fleet. Finally, we operationalized these patterns across the agent lifecycle, from pre-validated reference architectures and structured pipelines to a runtime governance agent that continuously evaluates deployed agents.

Industry observers note that our experience has shown these practices pay off in a few ways. Reusable templates and shared infrastructure reduced development costs. Teams also got agents to production faster, thanks to standard interaction models and automated deployment. Quality improved too, because the pipeline enforces proven patterns at every stage of the lifecycle.

Industry observers note that scaling agentic governance is an industry-wide imperative. The shift toward AI and generative-AI-supported workflow automation is already reshaping how engineering organizations operate. The winners will be those who move beyond experimentation and establish the discipline to govern autonomous agent networks at scale. With these practices in place, BMW engineers can focus on solving the problems that matter: Building the ultimate driving machine.

To apply these ideas to your own agents, start with the AWS Well-Architected Framework. This post used it as the model for reusable agent blueprints. To see how BMW codifies governance across its AWS environment, read How BMW Group uses automation to achieve end-to-end compliance at scale on AWS.

Recent findings suggest that the patterns and practices described in this post are a foundation, not a finish line. We are actively extending them across several fronts:.

Stephen Quinn joined the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) in 2004 and serves as a senior computer scientist in the Information Technology Laboratory (ITL). Mr. Quinn is the lead author for Integrating NIST risk management project work within the paradigm of Enterprise Risk Management (ERM). He is also program manager for the National Checklist Program and the National Online Informative Reference (OLIR) programs at NIST. He is a co-originator of the NIST Security Content Automation Protocol (SCAP).

Stephen was named to the “Federal 100” by the trade publication Federal Computer Week (FCW) and received the Department of Commence Gold Medal Award for his work in automating security protocols for applications. He also received the Federal CIO Council Leadership award for related work.

In a recent development, prior to joining NIST, Steve worked in the private sector as a consultant to the Department of Defense and large commercial outsourcings with Wall Street banking firms and insurance companies. Specifically, he comes from an operational background, having owned two companies that provided service offering for vulnerability assessments, designing security architectures, code development, risk management, certifications and accreditations, and ST&Es. His research experience and practitioner experience includes managing and remediating risks specific to computer viruses/malware, intrusion detection systems (IDSs), vulnerability/misconfiguration identification, categorization, and remediation.

#7489. Your Experts Have Partners. There's HOPE for Keeping Them Together

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1963 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Your Experts Have Partners. There's HOPE for Keeping Them Together

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1963 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have enabled state-of-the-art LLMs to be scaled to hundreds of billions of parameters, but they come with a fundamental and costly caveat: every expert MLP must occupy memory at inference time, even though the vast majority are idle for any given token.
  • Expert pruning is one of the most direct fixes to this memory bottleneck.
  • Existing pruning methods score each expert independently, assigning every expert a scalar importance score (based on a calibration dataset), and cutting out the least notable experts (in each layer independently).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have enabled state-of-the-art LLMs to be scaled to hundreds of billions of parameters, but they come with a fundamental and costly caveat: every expert MLP must occupy memory at inference time, even though the vast majority are idle for any given token. For example, Qwen3.5-122B has 256 experts in each of its 48 MoE layers, and 95% of its ~250 GB parameter memory footprint is taken up entirely by these expert MLPs alone. However, for any given token, only 8 experts in each layer are actually used.

Expert pruning is one of the most direct fixes to this memory bottleneck. That is, permanently delete the least useful experts. Pruning avoids the latency issues which make dynamic loading/off-loading of experts impractical; it does not require any training; and it composes with quantization. Given these attractive benefits and the simplicity of the idea, it's easy to see why expert pruning has become a go-to approach for shrinking MoEs. The difficulty lies in deciding which experts are safest to remove.

Existing pruning methods score each expert independently, assigning every expert a scalar importance score (based on a calibration dataset), and cutting out the least notable experts (in each layer independently). These are first-order methods, because they assume each expert's contribution is independent of all others. In reality, experts form cooperative groups. We observe consistent clusters of co-activated experts in our own experiments, and independent work has shown that expert cooperation is a stable property of MoEs and is important for model performance. Ignoring these interactions leads to suboptimal pruning, especially at aggressive rates.

Our newest paper derives HOPE (Higher-Order Pruning of Experts), a second-order method that accounts for pairwise expert interactions. At 50% pruning, HOPE achieves the best average rank of any method, with gains of up to +6.1% on agentic coding tasks over the next-best pruning method.

Recent findings suggest that in this post, we explain how HOPE works, show where it outperforms existing methods, and walk through how to use it for your own models. For readers unfamiliar with MoE architectures, see Mixture of Experts (MoEs) in Transformers.

In a standard MoE, each layer has EEE experts, and each input token xxx is routed independently to KKK such experts ( K=8 K = 8 K=8 is a typical choice). Routing is performed by a single layer which produces softmax-normalized gate weights gk(x)g_{k}(x)gk​(x) for each expert kkk, wherein the KKK experts with the highest gate weights are selected to form the active set of experts, T(x)⊂{1,..,E}T(x) \subset\{1,..,E\}T(x)⊂{1,..,E}. The output of the layer is then ∑k∈T(x)gk(x)fk(x)\sum\limits_{k\in T(x)}g_{k}(x)f_{k}(x)k∈T(x)∑​gk​(x)fk​(x), where fk(x)f_{k}(x)fk​(x) is the output of expert kkk for token xxx.

Sources indicate that left: typical MoE layer, where each token is routed to the top-K experts. Right: first-order methods rank and delete experts based on a scalar importance score, but the best pruning decisions will also consider the strength of interactions between experts.

Industry observers note that importantly, experts in the selected set T(x)T(x)T(x) are not independent. Experts form stable cooperative groups that get consistently co-activated together. This has been observed before in the literature, as well: expert co-selection patterns emerge early in training and stabilize throughout.

Industry observers note that this means that when we prune experts from an MoE layer, pruning decisions need to consider the higher-order effects between these experts. Removing expert A might seem fine on its own, but if expert B—which frequently cooperates with and relies on A—is highly notable, then removing A would dismantle a cooperative group just through a single deletion. First-order methods miss this entirely, because they score A and B separately.

This effect compounds at high pruning rates. When we remove up to 50% of experts, we risk breaking many cooperative links. This is where second-order pruning is most advantageous.

(See Appendix A in our corresponding paper for the full derivation of the HOPE objective).

According to recent reports, when we delete a set of PPP experts from some MoE layer, the selected set of experts T(x)T(x)T(x) (for any token xxx) can change. The pruned experts that would have been selected are replaced by the experts with the next-highest gate weights. The resulting change in layer output is the pruning error. Our goal is to find the prune-set PPP (of some predefined pruning budget ∣P∣\vert P\vert∣P∣) that minimizes the resulting pruning error (over tokens xxx from our calibration set).

Recent findings suggest that unfortunately, minimizing the pruning error over PPP directly is intractable. The pruning error depends on the identities of the replacement experts, which in turn depend on the prune-set PPP itself. HOPE sidesteps this by defining a tractable surrogate ZZZ, which strictly upper-bounds the dominant component of the pruning error:.

Z=[∑j∈P∩T(x)gj(x)∥fj(x)∥2]2≥true errorZ = \bigl[\sum\limits_{j \in P\cap T(x)} g_{j}(x)\Vert f_j(x)\Vert_{2}\bigr]^{2} \geq \text{true error}Z=[j∈P∩T(x)∑​gj​(x)∥fj​(x)∥2​]2≥true error.

In a recent development, because ZZZ is a squared sum, expanding it naturally produces cross-terms gi(x)gj(x)∥fi(x)∥2∥fj(x)∥2g_{i}(x)g_{j}(x)\Vert f_{i}(x)\Vert_{2}\Vert f_{j}(x)\Vert_{2}gi​(x)gj​(x)∥fi​(x)∥2​∥fj​(x)∥2​ between pairs of experts. These are the interaction terms that first-order methods discard.

To find the optimal prune-set, HOPE minimizes E[Z]\mathbb{E}[Z]E[Z] over the calibration set, which can be reformulated as the following quadratic program:.

P∗=arg min⁡p  p⊤Fps.t.p∈{0,1}E,∑k=1Epk=∣P∣P^{*} = \argmin_{p}\; p^{\top}Fp \quad \text{s.t.} \quad p \in \{0,1\}^{E}, \sum\limits_{k=1}^{E}p_{k} = \vert P\vertP∗=pargmin​p⊤Fps.t.p∈{0,1}E,k=1∑E​pk​=∣P∣.

where F∈RE×EF\in\mathbb{R}^{E\times E}F∈RE×E is defined as:.

Fi,j=1∣Xi,j∣∑x∈Xi,jgi(x)gj(x)∥fi(x)∥2∥fj(x)∥2whereXi,j={x:i,j∈T(x)}F_{i,j} = \frac{1}{\vert \mathcal{X}_{i,j}\vert} \sum\limits_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{i,j}} g_{i}(x)g_{j}(x)\Vert f_{i}(x)\Vert_{2}\Vert f_{j}(x)\Vert_{2}\quad\text{where}\quad \mathcal{X}_{i,j} = \{x: i,j \in T(x)\}Fi,j​=∣Xi,j​∣1​x∈Xi,j​∑​gi​(x)gj​(x)∥fi​(x)∥2​∥fj​(x)∥2​whereXi,j​={x:i,j∈T(x)}.

In a recent development, this F-matrix is collected on the calibration dataset, and the optimal prune-set is obtained by solving the resulting quadratic program (QP) with a continuous relaxation (then rounding to binary solutions). Each entry Fi,jF_{i,j}Fi,j​ captures the average gate-weighted output product of experts iii and jjj, across tokens where both are co-activated. Whereas the diagonal Fk,kF_{k,k}Fk,k​ measures individual expert importance, the off-diagonal entries ( Fi,jF_{i,j}Fi,j​ for i≠ji\neq ji=j) measure pairwise cooperative contribution.

What does FFF look like in practice? It reveals the structure of expert cooperation, which depends on layer:.

According to recent reports, visualization of the interaction matrix F for GLM-4.5-Air (128 experts per layer, 106B parameters total) at three representative layers (early, middle, late). Experts have been clustered to reveal block structure. Bright blocks along the diagonal indicate groups of experts with strong pairwise interaction scores.

In terms of practical cost, HOPE requires the same calibration pass as any other expert-pruning method (one forward pass over calibration data). The only addition is solving the quadratic program, which is non-convex, but can be solved efficiently via a standard QP solver (1–2 seconds each layer). The total additional overhead is negligible compared to first-order methods, as the time for calibration dominates.

Notably, HOPE has a strong connection to Router-weighted Expert Activation Pruning (REAP), a state-of-the-art first-order expert-pruning method. HOPE's F-matrix encodes individual expert importance scores on the diagonal, and this diagonal effectively recovers the scores used by REAP to independently rank experts for pruning (differing only by the variance of expert contributions). The diagonal of FFF recovers REAP's expert rankings almost perfectly (Spearman ρ=0.988\rho = 0.988ρ=0.988). Thus, any improvement HOPE achieves over REAP is attributable to the second-order interaction terms in the off-diagonal entries of the FFF-matrix.

Industry observers note that we evaluated HOPE as an expert pruning method using 3 models (Qwen3.5-122B, Qwen3.5-35B, and GLM-4.5-Air), with 2 calibration datasets (Evol-CodeAlpaca and SWE-Bench Verified trajectories). We used the Tulu3 suite and SWE-Bench Pro (agentic coding) to test the resulting pruned models, comparing HOPE to 4 first-order baselines (REAP, MAN, EAN, and Frequency) across pruning rates spanning from 10% to 50%.

Industry observers note that HOPE achieves the best overall rank across conditions and dominates at aggressive pruning rates. Left: average rank (lower = better) across all models, calibration sets, and benchmarks. Right: SWE-Bench Pro performance on Qwen3.5-35B.

According to recent reports, across all conditions, HOPE achieved the best average rank (2.07 out of 5 methods), with the highest rate of top-1 finishes (39% of conditions) and top-2 finishes (67%). In a head-to-head comparison, HOPE beats every other baseline in the majority of conditions.

As expected, HOPE's advantage grows at higher pruning rates. As more experts are removed, more cooperative links are broken, and the off-diagonal terms of FFF become more key. At 50% pruning, HOPE's average rank improves to 1.58 (vs. 2.42 for the next-best method, REAP). This is also the most deployment-relevant setting, where memory savings are large enough to accommodate longer contexts, deeper reasoning, and more tool calls.

Sources indicate that HOPE's advantage is most pronounced on SWE-Bench Pro, an agentic coding benchmark where models must solve real GitHub problems autonomously. These problems involve compositionally diverse tasks (e.g. coding, tool calls, reasoning, etc.) over many turns and likely exercise diverse expert combinations—exactly the regime where preserving cooperative structure matters most. On Qwen3.5-35B-A3B at 50% pruning, HOPE achieved 42.3 on SWE-Bench Pro, matching the unpruned model's 41.8 (while REAP dropped to 36.2, a 13% regression).

Notably, pruned models can occasionally match or exceed the unpruned baseline, likely because the removal of low-relevance experts reduces noise on the target tasks. This effect is not unique to HOPE and has been observed across pruning methods. Furthermore, our experiments highlighted that code-focused calibration with any pruning method (including HOPE) did not severely degrade non-coding benchmarks, and HOPE performed well across the Tulu3 suite regardless of calibration set.

Average strength of cooperation (measured by F-matrix value) with retained experts, split by experts on which HOPE and REAP disagree.

HOPE's advantage stems from optimizing over the entire interaction matrix FFF. To understand how this affects pruning decisions in practice, we examine the experts where HOPE and REAP disagree. For each disputed expert, we compute its cooperative score (i.e. its average F-value with other retained experts). Experts retained only by HOPE consistently have higher cooperative scores than experts retained only by REAP. In other words, as part of the QP optimization, HOPE sacrifices some individually high-scoring experts in favor of preserving cooperative clusters. The gains in benchmark performance (shown above) validate that this trade-off is advantageous.

Sources indicate that we created a basic package to run HOPE. It has three steps: 1) calibrate; 2) solve; 3) prune. Our package has been tested on Qwen3, Qwen3-Next, Qwen3.5, and GLM-4.5.

The calibration step runs a single forward pass over calibration data, whether it be agentic rollouts or single-turn traces. This uses HuggingFace transformers to hook into the forward pass of each individual MoE layer. For each token, this records which experts are selected, their gate weights, output norms, and pairwise co-activation statistics. The output of this step is the F-matrix, stored in an HDF5 file.

In a recent development, this command materializes the F-matrix and solves the binary quadratic program via a continuous relaxation. This takes a few seconds per layer, and the output is a JSON file which contains the prune-set. This is technically the final output of the HOPE algorithm.

Recent findings suggest that to complete the pipeline, we run this command to actually create the smaller model checkpoint from the prune-set. The pruned model is a standard HuggingFace checkpoint which is smaller on disk and in memory (no changes to vLLM or SGLang model definitions needed).

We also released a more compact Python API:.

HOPE's advantage is most pronounced at higher pruning rates (40–50%). At lower pruning rates (10–20%), first-order methods like REAP and MAN are sometimes competitive, and HOPE's advantage shrinks. Additionally, as with most expert-pruning algorithms, HOPE prunes each layer independently and does not account for cross-layer interactions. In our paper, we presented a theoretical framework for cross-layer HOPE, but the results remain preliminary. Finally, HOPE captures pairwise interactions, but even higher-order interactions (triplets and beyond) could provide additional signal, although they are combinatorially difficult to estimate.

For more information, see our corresponding paper and codebase.

Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18916.

Code: https://github.com/awslabs/HOPE.

To see how HOPE can be applied to next-generation hybrid architectures, see our corresponding repository.

Latest Update: Enable AI agents to pay for AWS Marketplace x402 products with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1493 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, when Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments became generally available in August 2026, agents could autonomously pay for paid APIs, MCP servers, and web content over open protocols like x402 and MPP with payment limits and full observability.
  • Figure 1: Overview of AgentCore payments showing the newly introduced AWS Billing integration for purchasing on AWS Marketplace.
  • Developers can also configure and automate discovery through the AWS Marketplace connector in AgentCore Gateway.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, when Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments became generally available in August 2026, agents could autonomously pay for paid APIs, MCP servers, and web content over open protocols like x402 and MPP with payment limits and full observability. Today we extend that autonomy to AWS Marketplace, so agents can discover and buy x402-enabled software, APIs, data, and content, and pay in USD on the agent developer’s AWS bill, removing the need for stablecoin wallets or API keys.

Figure 1: Overview of AgentCore payments showing the newly introduced AWS Billing integration for purchasing on AWS Marketplace.

Developers can also configure and automate discovery through the AWS Marketplace connector in AgentCore Gateway. Existing guardrails carry over, developers can set spending limits and approved sellers using AgentCore policy, and the payment session cap is enforced by AgentCore payments, so an agent is unable to overspend. Transactions are auditable in AWS CloudTrail and AWS Cost Explorer. Because agent purchases run through AWS accounts on both sides, agentic purchasing meets the security and auditability enterprises expect.

The x402 catalog on AWS Marketplace is expanding with a growing roster of trusted, verified sellers. Tavily, a live search provider for agentic commerce, is one of them:.

Agentic commerce isn’t just about giving agents the ability to pay. It’s about giving enterprises the confidence to let them.

Industry observers note that that conviction is driving Tavily’s collaboration with the AWS team on the design of Agentic Commerce. By bringing secure, x402 powered transactions to AWS Marketplace and connecting agents with trusted, KYC verified providers, AWS is laying the foundation for autonomous commerce at production scale.

This is what enterprise ready agentic commerce looks like.

— Rotem Weiss, Founder & CEO, Tavily.

Sources indicate that today’s launch adds AWS Billing as a payment option in AgentCore payments. An agent can now pay x402-enabled AWS Marketplace sellers per request, in USD, settling on their AWS bill.

When an AWS Marketplace seller responds with 402 Payment Required, its response includes a signed quote for the purchase. With AWS Billing, the agent can forward the seller’s x402 response to AgentCore payments. AgentCore payments checks session budgets, then returns a payment token. The agent retries the request to the seller with the payment token included and receives a successful response. AWS bills the charge to the AWS account where Payment Manager is set up, and the charge appears on that account’s AWS bill.

Industry observers note that to set up AWS Marketplace purchasing, the developer creates a Payment Manager with an AWS Billing connector. The connector only requires you to set up a service-linked role to access AWS Marketplace. Then, for each task, developers can create a payment session with a spending limit and give the agent the session ID.

Sources indicate that an agent’s first purchase from a seller creates an agreement for the AWS account with that seller, and AWS Marketplace automatically tracks later purchases against it. Each product will then show up as an AWS Marketplace line item. If your organization uses Private Marketplace, agents can only buy the products it allows.

In a recent development, in addition, to discover new sellers, we are launching a new AWS Marketplace connector in AgentCore Gateway. This optional integration helps agents find products and their endpoints. At launch, AWS Billing supports the x402 exact scheme, where the seller quotes a fixed price for each request.

According to recent reports, in this post, we walk through a research agent that discovers a tool, pays for a single request through AWS Billing, and answers with sources, with nothing set up in advance. We also provide an accompanying GitHub sample that you can use to evaluate the setup in your own AWS account.

Suppose a financial analyst asks the agent what was unveiled about agentic payments this week. The model wasn’t trained on this week’s news, so the agent looks for a search tool. Through AgentCore Gateway, it searches AWS Marketplace, reads the listing from Tavily, an AWS Marketplace seller, and requests the listing’s x402 endpoints.

In a recent development, the agent calls the endpoint and receives an x402 payload with price details. The agent then forwards the x402 payload to AgentCore payments. AgentCore payments checks it against the remaining session budget and returns a payment token. Once these checks are passed, the agent sends the request again with the token attached, and gets the search results. Its answer includes sources and states what it bought and what it cost.

In this workflow, agents can apply their reasoning to decide which AWS Marketplace tool to use.

Figure 2: End-to-end flow of the sample solution using a Strands agent.

1. Discover. The agent calls three read-only gateway tools in order: search listings, get a listing, and list its fulfillment options. Search listings tool only returns endpoints that accept x402. The last call returns the seller’s endpoint URL and the payment protocols it accepts.

It has been revealed that 2. Get a quote. The agent calls the endpoint with no payment attached. The seller answers with HTTP 402 and puts a signed quote in the PAYMENT-REQUIRED header. AWS Marketplace checks the signature against the seller’s registered key, which means a quote with an altered price gets rejected.

3. Pay. The agent passes the quote to the ProcessPayment API with the payment type AWS_BILLING_X402. If budget remains in the session, AgentCore payments issues a payment token. If not, the call fails and the developer is not charged.

4. Redeem. The agent sends the request again, this time with the token in the PAYMENT-SIGNATURE header, and the seller returns the content. Payment tokens are valid for about five minutes, so the agent completes steps 2 through 4 in a single pass.

5. Settle. On the developer’s first purchase from a seller, AWS Marketplace creates the agreement with that seller. After that it meters each charge to their AWS bill. Settlement runs asynchronously and demonstrates up in their AWS bill monthly.

Industry observers note that to create an AWS Billing connector, developers’ AWS accounts must have the AWS Marketplace service-linked role AWSServiceRoleForMarketplaceAgenticCommerce. AWS Marketplace uses this role to bill AWS Marketplace purchases that their agents make to their AWS account. Refer to the documentation for more details.

The open-source GitHub sample in the agentcore-samples repository runs through a demo of the newly introduced functionality. It can help you configure AgentCore payments for AWS Marketplace, connect Tavily, run the agent, and inspect the transaction. You can refer to the documentation for more details.

setup_aws_billing.py creates a payment manager with an AWS Billing connector, plus the AWS Marketplace service-linked role and three separate AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles. The session role can set budgets but can’t pay. Meanwhile the agent role can pay but can’t create sessions, so the agent has no way to raise its own budget.

Recent findings suggest that setup_gateway.py creates an AgentCore Gateway with the AWS Marketplace connector and gives the agent role the appropriate permissions to use it. The gateway’s role is limited to three read-only AWS Marketplace actions. If you choose to skip this step, you can instead set SELLER_URL in the environment variables to the seller’s endpoint, and the agent will pay that URL only rather than using AgentCore Gateway discovery.

It has been revealed that the script creates a payment session as the session role and then runs the agent as the agent role. By default the session budget is $0.05 and the per-request cap is $0.02.

According to recent reports, the agent searches, looks at listings, gets an endpoint, and pays once. In this test run against a $0.01 seller, it compared two listings before buying:.

Recent findings suggest that when the run finishes, the sample will print the payment with its amount, AWS Marketplace product ID, and processPaymentId. The AWS Marketplace meters charges asynchronously, so the Tavily line item takes a moment to appear on your bill. Agent purchases will also show up in AWS CloudTrail and AWS Cost Explorer.

According to recent reports, run cleanup.py to delete resources. Make sure to validate deletion to avoid incurring additional resource charges.

AgentCore payments and AWS Marketplace provide the infrastructure for agents that can transact. The research agent in this post goes from “I need live web search” to sourcing an answer on its own, discovering premium paid content through tools, and paying for requests that settle on the developer’s AWS bill.

Sources indicate that with AgentCore payments, developers can build with open protocols like x402, which opens them to a growing catalog of trusted, verified AWS Marketplace sellers. This gives agents more autonomy and developers more control. Governance is built in, with per-session spending caps and an approved seller list using AgentCore policy, and IAM identities that make it auditable in AWS CloudTrail and AWS Cost Explorer. The agent chooses the right tool for the task, and developers can keep the same billing, budgets, and controls they already trust.

Decision Models in Hugging Face

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2159 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Large Language Models (LLMs) are exceptionally good at generating text.
  • Consider a customer support system receiving the following message:.
  • "I was charged twice for my subscription.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Large Language Models (LLMs) are exceptionally good at generating text. We use them to answer questions, write code, reason about problems, and so much more. But not every problem requires generating text.

Consider a customer support system receiving the following message:.

"I was charged twice for my subscription. I need a refund today.".

The system needs to determine which team should handle the request, how urgent it is, and whether the customer is requesting a refund.

We could ask an LLM to return a JSON object containing these answers.

But what if the model could directly evaluate the available options and return a probability distribution over them, without generating any text?

This is the key idea behind decision models.

Sources indicate that A decision model takes some input context (state), evaluates a question with a set of predefined possible answers (primitives), and returns a structured decision along with probabilities. Instead of asking a model to generate an answer token by token, we ask it to assign probabilities to the answers that our application already understands.

Recent findings suggest that typeSafe AI introduced Jev, describing it as a System One model. The name draws inspiration from the distinction between fast, intuitive thinking (System 1) and slower, deliberative thinking (System 2).

Recent findings suggest that the community has converged to the term decision model, because it describes the model's computational role rather than invoking a particular theory of cognition. In the rest of the post we will refer to the models as "decision models" instead of "system one models". (A poll on twitter deciding what we should be calling such models).

For a decision model, the fundamental interface is:.

We could simply prompt an LLM to return a JSON object containing our decisions. In fact, this is how many applications already use language models for classification, routing, and other structured tasks.

However, there are a few problems with this approach.

Before understanding the interface of a decision model, it is useful to revisit two closely related approaches namely traditional classification and zero-shot classification.

Suppose we train a classifier that routes customer-support requests to three departments:.

Industry observers note that A conventional classification model learns a mapping from an input to a predefined set of labels. During training, the model learns to predict these labels from examples. A classification head typically produces one logit per class, and softmax turns those logits into a probability distribution.

The limitation here is that the output classes are baked into the model's classification head.

If we introduce a fourth department, such as Legal, the existing classifier does not automatically acquire a corresponding output class. We may need to modify the head, collect training data, and retrain or adapt the model.

Sources indicate that zero-shot classification addresses an important part of this limitation. Instead of requiring the classifier to be trained specifically on every output category, we supply the candidate labels at inference time.

Unlike a conventional fixed-label classifier, the categories can change from one request to another. Let’s add another department, such as “Legal”, and see the model outputs.

Sources indicate that one common implementation uses a model trained for natural language inference (NLI). Each candidate label is converted into a hypothesis, and the model measures how strongly the input entails that hypothesis.

It has been revealed that this already sounds quite similar to a decision model. And in many ways, it is.

Decision models extend this idea beyond simply assigning an input to a category. A decision model can accept several named questions about the same state, with different answer types. The types can be choosing between alternatives (choice), scoring an ordered scale (score), or estimating the probability that a statement is true (noul).

More importantly, its interface is designed around the probability distribution over possible decisions.

Consider these three approaches:.

Industry observers note that the advantage of decision models is not that they invented runtime-defined labels or probabilistic classification. It is that they organize these capabilities into a consistent interface, potentially backed by architectures and training procedures optimized specifically for decisions.

A decision model request has the following two components:.

According to recent reports, the state is the information the model should evaluate. It may be a string, a structured JSON object, or, other modalities for supported omni-modal models.

Sources indicate that questions describe what we want to know about the state. In the decision models interface, three fundamental primitives represent different forms of decisions:.

Choice is the most intuitive primitive and the closest to traditional classification.

Which department should handle this customer request?

The available options are Billing, Technical support, and Sales.

The model assigns a logit to each option. For logits z1,…,zKz_1,\ldots,z_Kz1​,…,zK​, (with KKK classes) we can obtain the probabilities using softmax:.

pi=exp⁡(zi)∑j=1Kexp⁡(zj) p_i=\frac{\exp(z_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(z_j)} pi​=∑j=1K​exp(zj​)exp(zi​)​.

Here, KKK is the number of choices.

Consider this illustrative distribution:.

Recent findings suggest that ∑i=1Kpi=1. \sum_{i=1}^{K}p_i=1. i=1∑K​pi​=1.

The model chooses the option with the largest probability:.

y^=arg⁡max⁡ipi \hat y=\arg\max_i p_i y^​=argimax​pi​.

In this case, the choice is Billing, with the probability of 0.998, but the remaining probabilities are useful too. They tell us how the model distributes its belief among the alternatives.

Choice works when there are several distinct alternatives. But what if we want to measure something on an ordered scale?

How urgent is this customer request?

The model again produces a probability distribution:.

Rather than returning only the most likely level, the Score primitive computes the expected value of the level index.

For a random variable XXX representing the level, the expectation is:.

E[X]=∑i=0K−1ipi \mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_{i=0}^{K-1}ip_i E[X]=i=0∑K−1​ipi​.

E[X]=0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7 \mathbb{E}[X] = 0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7 E[X]=0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7.

The reported score is therefore 1.7.

Recent findings suggest that this does not mean that the model selected a fictional level halfway between medium and high. It means that the expectation of its probability distribution is 1.7.

The third primitive is Noul, which represents a binary question.

Is the customer requesting a refund?

Rather than defining a list of choices, we ask the model to return the probability that the answer is true. We can understand this using the Bernoulli distribution (noul comes from Bernoulli).

Let YYY represent a binary outcome:.

Y∼Bernoulli⁡(p) Y\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p) Y∼Bernoulli(p).

According to recent reports, P(Y=1)=p,P(Y=0)=1−p. P(Y=1)=p,\qquad P(Y=0)=1-p. P(Y=1)=p,P(Y=0)=1−p.

it assigns a probability of 0.92 to Yes and 0.08 to No.

Recent findings suggest that the model is not randomly sampling a binary answer here. It returns the probability parameter itself, leaving the application to decide how to act on it.

Recent findings suggest that so far, we have obtained probability distributions from the model. But the decision model interface also returns a field called confidence for Choice and Score.

The full distribution might contain several possible answers, and it is useful to summarize how concentrated the model's belief is. With confidence we achieve just that.

For a Choice with KKK options, the confidence is:.

pmax⁡−1K1−1K \frac{p_{\max}-\frac{1}{K}}{1-\frac{1}{K}} 1−K1​pmax​−K1​​.

where pmax⁡p_{\max}pmax​ is the largest predicted probability.

In our previous three-choice example, Billing had probability 0.998:.

C=3(0.998)−12=0.997 C=\frac{3(0.998)-1}{2}=0.997 C=23(0.998)−1​=0.997.

Notice that the winning probability is 0.998, but the reported confidence is 0.997. The confidence normalizes the largest probability relative to the number of available options. In contrast, the ordered Score example only had a confidence of 0.558.

It has been revealed that decision models are a young and fast-moving space. Each one makes decisions differently under the hood (heads that score the whole schema jointly, separate readouts on top of LLM backbones, edge-sized and multimodal variants, etc). This variety is healthy, but it comes at a cost. If every model exposes its own interface, every tool around it needs model-specific adaptations.

According to recent reports, our goal at Hugging Face is to agree on a common interface without forcing a common implementation. A decision model should be free to work however it likes internally, as long as it accepts the same state and questions and returns the same typed decisions. Once that contract exists, the rest of the ecosystem can build on it once:.

The rest of this section walks through each of these pieces.

According to recent reports, transformers now supports the DecisionPipeline, AutoModelForDecision, and the DecisionConfig classes. These follow the same overall structure of the pipeline and model classes in transformers but are tailor made for decision models.

One can also inspect the configuration and the model like so:.

Transformers also supports the /v1/systemone endpoint.

We can start a local server using the serving dependencies:.

Using a compatible version of Transformers, we can then send a decision request:.

The response contains three named answers with the corresponding typed results and probabilities.

An interesting detail is that the above APIs works with compatible autoregressive language models too. Transformers constructs the decision prompts, evaluates the answer label logits in a batched forward pass, and applies softmax without generating response text. This means we can experiment with the decision interface without necessarily training a new model.

llama.cpp also supports decision models using the same /v1/systemone API.

For example, we can launch a GGUF decision model from the Hub:.

The default server runs on port 9931.

We can then send a request containing the same state and questions, using http://localhost:9931/v1/systemone. With the model selected by the server, we can omit the model field from the request.

The useful property is interface compatibility.

Recent findings suggest that hugging Face introduced a dedicated decision-model tag for discovering compatible models. This is useful because decision models do not have to share a single backbone or architecture.

For example, the ecosystem includes models based on encoder architectures such as ModernBERT, as well as models derived from larger generative language-model backbones.

Once we understand inference, the next question is whether we can adapt a decision model. Since decision models are integrated in transformers, we can fine-tune them with the Trainer API.

Below is a toy example that fine-tunes JEV-9B to route support requests. It is intentionally small, but it reveals the parts that matter:.

First-class support for training decision models is also coming to TRL (huggingface/trl#8040), so we won't have to write this plumbing by hand. At the time of writing, the PR is still open.

If we want to go further and turn a generative LLM into a decision model, Unsloth provides a recipe that fine-tunes models such as Qwen with LoRA and a decision-scoring head.

Decision models are interesting not because classification is upcoming, but because they make decisions and probabilities first-class outputs for software.

In a recent development, traditional classifiers already produce probabilities, and zero-shot classifiers already allow runtime-defined categories. Decision models bring these ideas into a typed interface with multiple question primitives, non-generative scoring, and the possibility of specialized training for reliable, calibrated decisions.

Industry observers note that great write-up. The step the post leaves to the application, turning noul: 0.83 into an action, is where things get hard in production. It's usually a threshold (if p > 0.9), and it quietly goes stale: raw probabilities are rarely calibrated, the right cut-off depends on what a mistake costs, and the outcome that states whether the decision was right (a chargeback, a reassigned ticket) arrives days or months later.

Recent findings suggest that I'm building an open-source, self-hosted tool for that loop: trimset. It sits in front of any /v1/systemone server (so transformers serve or llama.cpp) with a one-line URL change. It logs every decision and joins the real outcome when it arrives. It calibrates per question and model, then compiles thresholds and an escalation band with a stated guarantee ("false passes ≤ 2% with 95% confidence"), which your app applies locally. It's pre-alpha; drift and silent-upgrade alerts come next.

Live demo on recorded data, threshold simulator included: https://demo.trimset.dev/#/questions/refund_fraud/simulator.

For anyone running decision models in production: how do you pick your cut-offs today?

"Not because x, but because y" is very AI-sloppy language.

It has been revealed that the advantage of decision models is not that they invented runtime-defined labels or probabilistic classification. It is that they organize these capabilities into a consistent interface.

Nobody thinks that, literally. What I mean by that is, nothing capable of thinking would have written this sentence down because no thinking entity would suspect that decision models originated probabilistic classification. Only a non-thinking source of language, such as an LLM, might generate this sentence.

Decision models are interesting not because classification is new, but because they make decisions and probabilities first-class outputs for software.

Again, nobody thinks that, meaning only an LLM might generate this sentence.

The state + questions interface carries over to hosted decision models too. meraGPT Decider 1.1 takes the same shape through an API (model decider-1.1) rather than as open weights: up to 255 options per choice question, images in the state, and if you offer an "I don't know" option it takes it when the state doesn't support an answer. Against TypeSafe Jev 1.14 on the same items it's ahead on typed decisions, calibration and large label sets. Input is $0.04 per million tokens and output is free.

Introducing enhanced infrastructure observability in Amazon SageMaker HyperPod

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1529 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Large-scale model training is one of the most expensive workloads you can run on GPUs, and a single unhealthy accelerator can stall an entire distributed job.
  • Today, we are announcing enhanced observability in Amazon SageMaker HyperPod, a fresh capability that helps you diagnose GPU training concerns faster.
  • It has been revealed that diagnostic summary uses Amazon CloudWatch’s DetectGroupOutliers API to compare each GPU in a training job on utilization, memory, temperature, power, and SM clock, and flags GPUs that deviate from their peers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Large-scale model training is one of the most expensive workloads you can run on GPUs, and a single unhealthy accelerator can stall an entire distributed job. When training throughput drops, the hard part is rarely noticing that something is wrong. It is figuring out why and where. Teams often spend hours or days sifting through logs and disconnected dashboards to decide whether a slowdown came from a throttled GPU, a saturated network link, or a stalled data pipeline on the host.

Today, we are announcing enhanced observability in Amazon SageMaker HyperPod, a fresh capability that helps you diagnose GPU training concerns faster. It brings together diagnostic and profiling capabilities for training workloads that run on both Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) and Slurm orchestrators:.

It has been revealed that diagnostic summary uses Amazon CloudWatch’s DetectGroupOutliers API to compare each GPU in a training job on utilization, memory, temperature, power, and SM clock, and flags GPUs that deviate from their peers. Static diagnostic rules surface common failure patterns such as GPU hardware faults (XID errors, ECC memory errors), EFA throughput drops, thermal throttling, and overheating, so you catch degradation before it affects training.

Distributed training is expensive, and small inefficiencies compound into significant wasted GPU hours. Until now, getting visibility into HyperPod infrastructure meant stitching together separate tools, and even then, the metrics told you that performance had degraded without telling you why.

Enhanced observability closes three gaps. It isolates a single bad accelerator across hundreds or thousands of GPUs whether through XID errors, ECC memory faults, or thermal throttling, so you spend time on the fix instead of the search.

Together, these capabilities reduce troubleshooting time and help you keep expensive accelerators busy.

Each capability targets a different layer of a distributed training job.

Enhanced observability collects telemetry at two levels:.

According to recent reports, default metrics (enabled automatically) cover cluster health, CPU/disk/OS-level usage, GPU utilization and temperature, and per-job resource utilization. These metrics are collected every 30 seconds and sent to your chosen metric store with approximately 1–2% CPU overhead and 250–300 MB of memory.

Advanced metrics (opt-in) provide deeper visibility:.

Advanced metrics are optional because they increase the volume of telemetry sent to your metric store, which has a cost implication. Most customers running small jobs on small clusters may not need them, but they are essential for long-running training jobs on large clusters where patterns emerge over time.

You can choose between two metric stores:.

Previously, only Prometheus was supported. CloudWatch is now the default, offering lower pricing compared to Amazon Managed Service Prometheus and tighter integration with the SageMaker console.

The diagnostic summary uses two complementary approaches to surface problems across your HyperPod cluster.

According to recent reports, GPU outlier detection uses CloudWatch’s DetectGroupOutliers API to compare GPUs within a training job across utilization, memory usage, temperature, power draw, and SM clock frequency. When a GPU deviates significantly from its peers, it appears as an outlier card in the diagnostic summary. This works for both EKS and Slurm jobs.

Static diagnostic rules evaluate known failure patterns and organize detected challenges by type:.

Each detected issue identifies the affected job, cluster, node, accelerator, and rank.

Enhanced observability is delivered as an add-on for EKS-orchestrated clusters and as an extension for Slurm-orchestrated clusters, which means you control who can install or change it through AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM).

If you already have a cluster, you can use it. To create a new SageMaker HyperPod cluster, you can follow the step-by-step outline. In general, the steps are as follows:.

  • Hugging Face is where teams find, build and run open models: from hosting private models and datasets, to running GPU workloads with Jobs, deploying models with Inference Endpoints, calling thousands of models through Inference Providers, or hosting demos on GPU Spaces.

CVE-2024-27834 Apple Multiple Products Improper Authentication Vulnerability This type of vulnerability is a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and poses significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria. Aware of an exploited vulnerability not presently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • CISA, the Australian Signals Directorate’s Australian Cyber Security Centre (ASD’s ACSC) and the National Security Agency (NSA) released joint guidance and an accompanying quick-reference list to help organizations assess vendor readiness for transitioning to post-quantum cryptography (PQC).
  • Sources indicate that many organizations rely on third-party vendors for managed services, cloud capabilities, and other cryptography-dependent products and services.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, CISA, the Australian Signals Directorate’s Australian Cyber Security Centre (ASD’s ACSC) and the National Security Agency (NSA) released joint guidance and an accompanying quick-reference list to help organizations assess vendor readiness for transitioning to post-quantum cryptography (PQC). As quantum computing advances, widely used public-key cryptography will become vulnerable to compromise from cryptographically relevant quantum computers (CRQCs). To protect their systems and data, organizations must plan for and transition to PQC—which includes algorithms capable of withstanding both classical computing and quantum-enabled threats—before CRQCs become available. Many organizations rely on third-party vendors for managed services, cloud capabilities, and other cryptography-dependent products and services. Cryptography is also embedded in systems and devices that are difficult to enhancement, tied to long asset lifecycles, and require vendor support or replacement—such as industrial control systems and Internet of Things (IoT) devices. Reliance on vendors means that effective PQC transition depends on vendor readiness, and early, structured engagement with these vendors is critical to planning efforts. Organizations can use the vendor-neutral questions outlined in this guidance to determine whether a vendor understands quantum-related risks, maintains transparency over its cryptographic implementations, and supports a secure, cost-effective and timely transition to PQC. Visit CISA’s PQC Initiative page for additional resources.
