  • CISA has added six latest vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.
  • These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, CISA has added six newly introduced vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-20320 Cisco BroadWorks Improper Restriction of XML External Entity Reference Vulnerability  CVE-2026-111560 Barracuda Networks Multiple Products OS Command Injection Vulnerability  CVE-2026-111793 Openwave Messaging Limited Webtop Media Transcoder Incorrect Resource Transfer Between Spheres Vulnerability  CVE-2026-116606 Barracuda Networks Email Security Gateway (ESG) Authentication Bypass Using an Alternate Path or Channel Vulnerability  CVE-2026-124194 Microsoft Office Outlook Missing User Interaction for Potentially Unsafe Action Vulnerability  CVE-2026-125350 Google Chromium Use-After-Free Vulnerability  These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria. Aware of an exploited vulnerability not presently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

LLMON: An LLM-Native Markup Language, now in Granite 4.1 3B and 8B

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1703 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • LLMs rely on their context to generate the next set of tokens.
  • To address this, we developed LLMON (LLM Object Notation, pronounced “lemon”), an LLM-native markup language for explicitly communicating structure and semantics to the models.
  • Today we are releasing two experimental preview models, derived from Granite 4.1 base models, trained to consume and generate LLMON-marked text: granite-4.1-3b-LLMON-preview and granite-4.1-8b-LLMON-preview.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

LLMs rely on their context to generate the next set of tokens. Over a long trajectory, the context fills with numerous types of components: a system prompt, past conversation turns, instructions that act on retrieved documents, tool responses or user data, requirements constraining the allowed output, and reasoning chains. The context carries a rich structure, most of which is either implicit to the model or encoded in formats such as JSON that were not designed to be digested by LLMs. This is one of the main reasons LLMs, particularly those on the smaller end of the scale, are brittle and sometimes fail in unexpected ways. The lack of explicit structure can also be exploited by attackers, for example, in the form of prompt injections.

To address this, we developed LLMON (LLM Object Notation, pronounced “lemon”), an LLM-native markup language for explicitly communicating structure and semantics to the models. Semantically coherent components are marked with meaningful tags which are wrapped in reserved special-token delimiters. Data schemas, including nesting, are stated in a way that is unambiguous to a causal LLM. Unique IDs make it possible to point to specific instructions, which could reside anywhere in the context, and bind them to the data payloads they should act on, analogous to the way functions are called and arguments are passed to them in programming languages.

Today we are releasing two experimental preview models, derived from Granite 4.1 base models, trained to consume and generate LLMON-marked text: granite-4.1-3b-LLMON-preview and granite-4.1-8b-LLMON-preview. We are also releasing a GitHub repo, which includes a toolkit for working with LLMON and examples of workflows and templates.

JSON was designed for parsers, not for causal language models. The tokenizer is not constrained to respect the grammar, and structure is encoded by tokens ({, ", :) that may also appear in normal text. To a model, a quotation mark inside a document and a quotation mark that closes a field are the same token. Escaping rules that are clear to a parser are only statistical patterns to a model. Nesting depth is encoded by counting brackets, which transformers are known to be weak at, especially over long spans.

In a recent development, LLMON, on the other hand, is an XML-like markup whose structural delimiters are reserved special tokens rather than characters, so structure and content use separate parts of the vocabulary. Tags are stated at the beginning of each span, and the boundaries between spans are explicit. Nested structures are stated locally so the model does not need to keep track of the hierarchy over long spans.

Since most teams already have pipelines built around JSON, we created conversion tools and example notebooks that translate JSON to LLMON and back in a lossless manner.

Sources indicate that LLMON does not replace chat templates; rather, it enriches them. Where regular chat templates tell the model which part belongs to which role (system, user, assistant), LLMON tells it what each component means and how components relate to each other, within and across roles.

Recent findings suggest that the LLMON preview models ship with their own chat template, so you build the same messages list you would pass to any chat model and call apply_chat_template as usual; it renders the LLMON shown below. The only difference is that a turn can now name its parts and mark each one exec: True or False. A part marked True is bound into the exec block at the bottom of the rendered output, which states which instruction to run and what it operates on; a part marked False is still rendered into the context but is referenced by nothing.

Which the model receives as the following (with newlines and indentation added here for readability, as the template emits none):.

The two-character block IDs are drawn from a fixed set that this tokenizer encodes as single tokens, so addressing a block always costs two tokens regardless of which ID is drawn.

According to recent reports, the role is still a single user turn, but its components reach the model as five separate addressable blocks, bound together by a sixth (the exec block) that states: run this instruction, on this data, subject to these two requirements, and put the answer in the block named here, which is the same assistant block the model then fills. A conventional template would have flattened all components into one string and left the model to infer which part was the task, which was the subject, and which were constraints.

In a recent development, indirect prompt injection is a type of attack where a malicious instruction is hidden in a data payload, such as a retrieved document, a tool response, or user-provided data. This is the problem LLMON’s instruction/data separation is designed to address.

According to recent reports, we compared the LLMON previews against several open-source and closed-source models. We evaluated on the OPI benchmark, which places the injection in the data of classic NLP tasks. Several attack strategies are employed. We report robustness, defined as 1 − attack success rate: the share of attacks where the model does not carry out the injected instruction.

Sources indicate that all non-LLMON models are highly susceptible, carrying out the injected instructions with high probability. LLMON practically eliminates the problem on this benchmark, avoiding 47% more attacks relative to the best frontier model that we tested, and 95% more than the best open-source model. We observe similar trends on other benchmarks (ASB and StruQ). It is worth noting that these benchmarks test robustness to static indirect prompt injections. The instruction/data separation directly addresses this type of attack. We are actively working on also improving adaptive attacks which unfold over many chat turns.

Sources indicate that safety gains don’t come at the expense of general capability. Across standard benchmark categories, the LLMON models perform on par with the Granite 4.1 Instruct models.

Sources indicate that in short, if you’re experimenting with Granite 4.1 3B or 8B today, you can swap in the LLMON preview and should see comparable general performance with much stronger resistance to prompt injection. No conversion pipeline is required. Naming the turn's parts (e.g., instruction, data, requirement as in the example above) is enough. The shipped chat template turns those into LLMON blocks for you. Our LLMON-converters library goes one level deeper: if a part is itself structured, such as a JSON document, LLMONizing it preserves that structure as typed, individually addressable blocks, instead of one opaque string.

The models start from Granite 4.1 base checkpoints rather than the released instruct models, so LLMON behavior is learned during post-training rather than layered on an existing chat format.

In a recent development, LLMON defines six delimiters that mark the start and end of tags and allow nesting and anchoring; they are installed in the tokenizer as reserved single tokens. We re-serialized a conventional instruction-tuning corpus into LLMON: every prompt component becomes its own addressable block, and each turn carries an execution block naming which instruction to run, which inputs it operates on, and where the output goes. The task mix is the one a normal instruct model sees (chat, multi-turn, RAG, tool calling), which is why benchmark performance stays close to the conventionally tuned model. In addition, we augment the data with decoy instructions and data blocks that are present in context but deliberately left unbound, while the target output is unchanged. So the model learns to follow the dependencies dictated by the execution block and ignore the rest. Reinforcement learning follows: five sequential GRPO stages spanning multi-domain reasoning, RLHF, knowledge calibration, and math, followed by a final DPO stage on a thousand on-policy preference pairs built from the model’s own responses to injection attempts.

Sources indicate that the resulting privilege rule falls out of this layout rather than an added guardrail: an instruction reached through an execution block is authoritative, while anything reached as input (data, documents, tool schemas, tool results) is material to read, not a command to follow. Furthermore, instructions and data spans that are not called on in the execution block are ignored. This is a learned behavior, not an enforced guarantee. To see how this plays out in the attention layers of a LLMON model, try the LLMON Attention Visualization on Hugging Face Spaces.

LLMON is not tied to a fixed schema: you can choose tag names and structure that fit your domain and fine-tune an adapter to read and write them. We demonstrate this on ScienceWorld, a text-based benchmark where an agent carries out elementary science tasks (such as boiling water) by issuing one command at a time and receiving a score from the simulator. We defined a vocabulary capturing the structure in the planning trajectories involved in solving these tasks. The vocabulary includes tags such as instr.task.goal, req.planning_policy.rule, data.state.room, data.state.inventory and assistant.next_action. We rendered every step of ScienceWorld's reference solutions with these tags and tuned a LoRA on top of a LLMON model. The trained model then plays held-out games and writes its next action in the new vocabulary. This notebook walks through the full workflow, from converting reference trajectories to playing the test games and scoring the adapter against the untrained base model. Another example for tool-calling agents can be found in this notebook.

This is an experimental preview, ready for exploration and evaluation but not for production.

Tell us what you find: what worked, what broke, and which use cases you’d like to see. Post it in GitHub Discussions.

According to recent reports, that's really awesome! With an Apple pkl community renderer, you could potentially write PKL and render LLMON. 🥒🍋.

Any-to-pkl-community will convert json, yaml, toml to pkl, so just need the render part.

This is an interesting development, especially the idea of giving LLMs a more explicit structure for understanding instructions, data, and their relationships. The discussion about prompt injection and separating instructions from input data is particularly relevant as organizations build more advanced LLM applications. Implementing these approaches requires engineers who understand model behavior, fine-tuning, context management, and evaluation. I think these technical requirements are crucial when estimating the cost to hire an LLM engineer, particularly for specialized enterprise projects. I came across this resource that explores the different factors involved: https://mobisoftinfotech.com/resources/blog/cost-to-hire-llm-engineer-2026.

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1383 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Amazon ↗ Open Full Page

Introducing Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Global Inference Gateway: One endpoint across Regions and clusters

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1383 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • During a traffic peak, a request can sit in a queue on a saturated HyperPod cluster while GPUs on another cluster, sometimes in another AWS Region, sit idle.
  • Sources indicate that in Introducing Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference Gateway, we showed how the Inference Gateway gives each Amazon SageMaker HyperPod cluster a single, GPU-aware endpoint.
  • Today, SageMaker HyperPod introduces the Global Inference Gateway.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

During a traffic peak, a request can sit in a queue on a saturated HyperPod cluster while GPUs on another cluster, sometimes in another AWS Region, sit idle. You have already paid for that capacity, but your requests can’t reach it.

Sources indicate that in Introducing Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference Gateway, we showed how the Inference Gateway gives each Amazon SageMaker HyperPod cluster a single, GPU-aware endpoint. It reads real-time signals such as key-value (KV) cache utilization and queue depth to place every request on the best-suited pod. That solves routing inside one cluster, but not across clusters.

Today, SageMaker HyperPod introduces the Global Inference Gateway. It is one SageMaker-managed gateway that routes across every cluster you register, in one Region or across Regions. The gateway picks the cluster and carries the request over the AWS backbone, with automatic failover and authentication through AWS Signature Version 4 (SigV4) and AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM). Inside each cluster, the Inference Gateway keeps picking the pod, unchanged. The Global Inference Gateway is the second tier of the architecture we described in part 1.

Models are getting larger, and the GPU capacity to serve them is harder to find. To get enough of it, you spread it across more clusters and more Regions.

Consider a team that serves four models across five HyperPod clusters in two Regions. Without the Inference Gateway, clients track 20 endpoints: one per model per cluster. The Inference Gateway cuts that to five, one per cluster. But each client still picks a cluster itself.

The team needs one endpoint that sends each request to the best-suited cluster and moves traffic off a failed cluster on its own.

The Global Inference Gateway helps you get more from the GPU capacity you already have, with less to operate.

Recent findings suggest that “At Bagelcode, we run our own LLM inference service on AWS to help teams across the company, including our game teams, use AI to improve how they work. In our beta tests, the Global Inference Gateway in Amazon SageMaker HyperPod routed requests across two AWS Regions through a single endpoint and kept serving them when one cluster could no longer serve the model. That gave our small platform team cross-Region failover without having to build or maintain our own routing layer.”.

— Jinhyung Park, VP (AI Platform), Bagelcode.

Setting up the gateway takes two decisions: which clusters to open up for routing, and which of them to group behind one gateway.

A cluster is reachable only after you publish it. When you publish a cluster, the controller creates a Network Load Balancer in front of the cluster’s Inference Gateway, publishes a virtual private cloud (VPC) endpoint service on it, and uploads the listener’s certificate to your TLS bucket. These resources live in your account. If you list a cluster in a gateway before you publish it, the call fails with a message that tells you what to fix.

Figure 1 shows the path of each request: (1) your client signs the request with SigV4 and sends it to the gateway’s regional endpoint. (2) The gateway authenticates the caller and picks the best cluster. (3) AWS PrivateLink carries the request to that cluster, in the same Region or another, and (4) the cluster’s Inference Gateway routes it to a model pod, as it does today.

In a recent development, figure 1: The Global Inference Gateway receives each request at one regional endpoint and forwards it over AWS PrivateLink to the best HyperPod cluster, where the cluster’s Inference Gateway routes it to a model pod. Each cluster publishes its load back to the gateway.

It has been revealed that you decide which clusters to publish, which to group behind a gateway, and how to weight routing. AWS operates the rest:.

On each cluster, a service-managed metrics publisher with its own IAM role sends the cluster’s load to the gateway.

For each request, the gateway scores every healthy cluster on four signals and sends the request to the highest-scoring cluster. Each cluster’s metrics publisher supplies the load signals.

You control how much each signal counts with routing weights. Each weight is a value from 0.0 to 1.0, and a weight of 0 turns that signal off. If you set weights, you set all four, and they must add up to 1.0. If you omit them, the defaults in the following table apply.

The defaults favor clusters close to the gateway’s Region, while still moving traffic toward clusters with available capacity and away from clusters that are failing. If resilience matters more than proximity for your workload, raise ErrorRate and lower RegionProximity. For example, the following routing block weights recent errors at 0.7:.

You pass the weights in the Routing parameter of CreateGlobalInferenceGateway, and you can change them later with UpdateGlobalInferenceGateway.

Your path depends on what you run today. If you serve from a single cluster, stay on that cluster’s Inference Gateway endpoint. Move to the Global Inference Gateway when you add a second cluster.

To set up the Global Inference Gateway, you prepare each cluster, create an execution role, and call CreateGlobalInferenceGateway. You then send OpenAI-compatible requests, signed with SigV4, to the gateway endpoint. For step-by-step instructions, including the IAM roles and policies, see the AWS documentation.

Every request to the gateway is signed with SigV4 and authorized with IAM. Callers need permission to invoke the gateway, and streaming has its own action:.

Attach this policy to each IAM identity that sends requests. To allow every gateway in the account, use global-inference-gateway/* as the resource.

The execution role follows least privilege. It can describe only the clusters you list, reach only their Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) API, and read only the routing certificates under the gig/ prefix of your TLS bucket, tagged as created by HyperPod Inference.

Sources indicate that identity tokens. If your clusters check JSON Web Tokens (JWTs), pass the token with --customer-identity-token (the X-Amzn-SageMaker-Customer-Identity-Token header), with no Bearer prefix. The token travels inside the SigV4 signature, so an unsigned token is rejected with 403 and a repeated token with 400. Turn on JWT checks on every cluster that serves a model, or on none of them, so a request doesn’t succeed on one cluster and fail on another.

In a recent development, requests reach your clusters only through AWS PrivateLink, as shown in Figure 1. The gateway does not log or store prompts or completions.

Here are steps to configure the gateway.

Industry observers note that prepare the new cluster and create the execution role’s EKS access entry on it, as described in the documentation. Also add the new cluster to the Resource lists of the execution role’s permissions policy. Then call AddInferenceGateway in the gateway’s Region, even if the new cluster is in another Region:.

According to recent reports, the gateway validates the cluster and starts routing to it once it is healthy. The endpoint, other clusters, and clients aren’t affected.

Call RemoveInferenceGateway in the gateway’s Region:.

The gateway stops sending new requests to the cluster, lets in-flight requests finish, and removes the private endpoint. A gateway always keeps at least one cluster. To withdraw the cluster fully, set globalRouting.enabled: false in its InferenceGatewayConfig and reapply it.

Call DeleteGlobalInferenceGateway:.

According to recent reports, the gateway endpoint stops serving, and per-cluster endpoints keep serving. After the gateway is deleted, withdraw each cluster with globalRouting.enabled: false, then delete the execution role and the IAM permissions you added for global routing.

The following table summarizes how common events and changes affect traffic.

For any troubleshooting assistance, please see the Troubleshooting Guide.

In a recent development, in this post, we introduced the Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Global Inference Gateway: one SageMaker-managed endpoint across your HyperPod clusters, in one Region or several. The gateway picks the cluster based on KV cache headroom, queue depth, Region proximity, and error rate, and moves traffic off a failed cluster with no client changes.

In a recent development, the Global Inference Gateway is available in 13 AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (N. California), US West (Oregon), South America (São Paulo), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (Ireland), Europe (London), Europe (Stockholm), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Asia Pacific (Mumbai), Asia Pacific (Singapore), and Asia Pacific (Sydney).

To get started, see the AWS documentation.

General Recommendations Operators of critical power systems (e.g. TSOs or DSOs) worldwide are usually required by regulations to build resilience into the power grids by applying multi-level redundant secondary protection schemes. It is therefore recommended that the operators check whether appropriate resilient protection measures are in place. The risk of cyber incidents impacting the grid's reliability can thus be minimized by virtue of the grid design. Siemens strongly recommends applying the provided security updates using the corresponding tooling and documented procedures made available with the product. If supported by the product, an automated means to apply the security updates across multiple product instances may be used. Siemens strongly recommends prior validation of any security update before being applied, and supervision by trained staff of the update process in the target environment. As a general security measure Siemens strongly recommends protecting network access with appropriate mechanisms (e.g. firewalls, segmentation, VPN). It is advised to configure the environment according to our operational guidelines in order to run the devices in a protected IT environment. Recommended security guidelines can be found at: https://www.siemens.com/gridsecurity Additional Resources For further inquiries on security vulnerabilities in Siemens products and solutions, please contact the Siemens ProductCERT: https://www.siemens.com/cert/advisories Terms of Use The use of Siemens Security Advisories is subject to the terms and conditions listed on: https://www.siemens.com/productcert/terms-of-use. Recommended Practices CISA recommends consumers take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet. Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies. CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets. Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies. Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. This advisory covers the status of impact of various Siemens software products. Siemens is actively monitoring the situation and assessing the implications of these vulnerabilities on our portfolio. Because this evaluation is ongoing, our findings are subject to change as newly introduced technical details and vendor updates emerge. We will publish updated findings, guidance, and remediation recommendations as soon as they become available. Siemens has released new versions for several affected products and recommends to revision to the latest versions. Siemens is preparing further fixes and recommends mitigations for products where fixes are not or not yet available.

#7432. Latest Update: Welcome Inkling 2 Mini, Cutting-edge Performance for your Local Setup

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2445 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Welcome Inkling 2 Mini, Cutting-edge Performance for your Local Setup

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2445 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that TLDR; Inkling 2 Mini is a upcoming looped transformer model.
  • Inkling 2 Mini is much, much smaller than Inkling 2 Small, and is designed for local AI setups.
  • Sources indicate that we ship transformers, llama.cpp, and MLX support.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that TLDR; Inkling 2 Mini is a upcoming looped transformer model. It’s a multimodal Mixture-of-Experts with ~26B physical total and 3B active parameters per token. It uses a neat trick to increase capacity: some layers are visited in a loop that repeats three times, which makes it work like it had more parameters. It supports a 1M-token context size, accepts images and text inputs. Thinking Machines Lab ships the model in a mixed-precision format, with NVFP4 and MXFP8 expert weights. A DSpark drafter is also included for additional speed-up at a small memory cost.

Inkling 2 Mini is much, much smaller than Inkling 2 Small, and is designed for local AI setups. We think this is a refreshingly fresh great local model. In our vibe tests, it's at least comparable with Qwen 3.8 27B. More validation is needed, but we are super excited about this release!

Sources indicate that we ship transformers, llama.cpp, and MLX support. SGLang also provides day-zero inference support for production deployments on datacenter hardware.

This post goes through what makes Inkling Mini different, some of our vibe tests, and how you can use it with your setup.

Inkling 2 Mini is a mixture-of-experts model with 24 decoder layers, but the 12 middle layers run three times in a loop. Therefore, the model acts as if it had 48 (6+ 3*12 + 6) logical layers with just 24 physical ones.

Similar to Inkling 2 Small, Inkling 2 Mini executes 48 layer visits per token. The hidden size is 2,304 instead of 4,608. At each layer visit, both variants route the token to 8 experts, but Mini selects them from among 128 experts per layer, while Small selects from 384.The decoder runs layers 0–5 once, layers 6–17 three times, and layers 18–23 once. All three passes through layers 6–17 reuse the same weights.

It has been revealed that architectures such as Nanbeige have explored looping before. But Inkling 2 Mini explores an interesting approach. Every pass through the looped core (layers 6–17) starts from the same inputs which is the output of the first six layers. Information moves between passes through cross-pass messages. Each looped layer reads a message from the previous pass's outputs with its own learned query (one message for its query, key, value and MLP inputs). A small gating controller then looks at both the layer's current input and the message. It decides how much of the current input to forget and how much of the message to add. Each pass therefore refines what the previous one computed.

Text decoder width is 2,304, and the intermediate width of each expert is 1,152. Reusing core weights reduces the number of distinct layers the checkpoint stores. The model still executes all 48 visits, and each visit keeps its own KV and short-convolution state.

According to recent reports, in addition to the flagship Inkling 2 Mini model, a research artifact has also been released. It shares the same architecture, but this variant was trained to accept a variable number of passes through the loop 🤯. Setting 1 or 2 passes instead of 3 will make inference run a lot faster, but generations may be of slightly lower quality. We tested this variant, and it works, but we haven’t evaluated it in depth.

Industry observers note that inkling 2 Mini is state-of-the-art in its class in the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 (AAv5), as well as across many benchmarks in various categories. Compared with Gemma 4 31B, Muse Glimmer, Qwen3.8-27B, and Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, Inkling 2 Mini leads in 32 benchmarks out of 48. These cover coding and autoresearch, agentic search and tool use for knowledge work, vision interpretation and creation, reasoning and knowledge, and safety and alignment. See the Inkling 2 Mini model card for the full list of benchmarks and scores.

Inkling 2 Mini is a great local coding companion. It leads in FrontierCode v2.0, ties with Qwen3.8-27B on Terminal-Bench 4.0, and trails Qwen on AutomationBench-AA v1.0.6. You can check out a few of our highlights below for coding and knowledge work. Note that AA Briefcase is in ELO rating, higher is better.

In this section, you can find how to use Inkling 2 Mini in transformers, llama.cpp, MLX, and SGLang.

We provide support for both Inkling 2 Mini (fixed loop) and the TML-d24-varloop-research (variable loop) research variant.

You can use the AutoModelForMultimodalLM class.

According to recent reports, pass reasoning_effort="medium" to processor.apply_chat_template(...) to set the effort for a request. The chat template adds the numeric value to the prompt as a system message. The default is high (0.9).

According to recent reports, available levels are none (0.0), minimal (0.1), low (0.2), medium (0.7), high (0.9; default), xhigh (0.99), and max (0.99). You can also pass a number from 0.0 to 0.99, such as reasoning_effort=0.35.

According to recent reports, in this example we ask our model about the current temperature at a given location. With the prompt, we also provide the tool (get_current_temperature) to do it. The model asks for a tool call, we call the tool on its behalf and then add the output to the next instruction set. It uses the output of the tool and provides us with the final result.

If you want to know more about tool calling, we recommend going to our official docs.

One can also enable multimodality by setting --enable-multimodal.

SGLang can use a three-layer DSpark draft to propose tokens for the target model to verify. The draft reads the inputs to decoder visits 5, 23, and 41, plus the final normalized state at index 48. With the draft weights present, add --speculative-algorithm DSPARK --context-length 131072 to the server command.

We benchmarked the models with and without speculative decoding, and measured generation speed on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU where every request has a 1,024-token prompt and generates exactly 1,024 tokens and concurrency of 1, 4, 16 and 64.

We upstreamed MLX support to the mlx-lm project, including multimodal image and text inputs, and shared quants through the mlx-community organization.

According to recent reports, MLX inference works with the original checkpoint too. In this case, the native nvfp4 + mxfp8 quantization scheme is used without reconversion: you get the original quality the authors intended.

We have given Inkling 2 Mini a shot in many fun tasks, check them out in this section.

The same prompt produced two sunset flythroughs over procedural mountains and reflective water, each rendered with a single WebGL fragment shader.

According to recent reports, build the most impressive original real-time scene you can: a slow, cinematic camera flight over procedural mountains, through volumetric clouds and low over water with reflections, all lit by a sunset. Deliver it as a single self-contained index.html in the current directory that renders everything in one full-screen WebGL fragment shader, purely from code (no textures, images, fonts, libraries, external files or network requests of any kind). It must run smoothly in desktop Chrome at 1920x1080, aiming for 60 fps on a desktop GPU, with an automatic resolution-scale fallback that lowers the internal render resolution when the frame rate drops, and the flight must keep going indefinitely without glitches. To check your work, run node shot.cjs index.html shot.png 6 (the third argument is how many seconds to wait; a comma list such as 3,12,25 saves one screenshot per time, and an optional fourth argument sets the size, default 1280x720): it renders the page in headless Chrome, saves the screenshot(s), and prints the WebGL renderer, a rough frame rate and any console errors; then look at the images. The headless renderer on this machine may be software-only, so its frame rate can be far below what a real desktop GPU achieves and is not the target. Decide for yourself when the result is finished, then reply with a short description of what you built.

Vincent van Gogh, The Starry Night (1889).

Sources indicate that we gave Inkling 2 Mini a reference image of Van Gogh’s painting and a screenshot helper in the Pi coding harness. Inkling wrote a self-contained HTML page with a single WebGL2 fragment shader. The shader draws the scene from code without loading the reference image or any other assets. It uses time to animate the swirling sky, the glow of the stars, the swaying cypress, and the flicker of the village windows.

Inkling rendered and reviewed its work over 24 rounds of screenshot checks. We recorded the final animation frame by frame at 1080p and 60 fps on an Apple M4 Max.

In this folder, starry-night.jpg is Vincent van Gogh's The Starry Night (1889, public domain). Recreate it as a living painting: a single self-contained index.html (all code inline, no external files, libraries or network requests) that fills the browser window and runs smoothly in desktop Chrome at 1920x1080. Everything must be generated procedurally in code, for example with WebGL shaders; the page must not load, embed or sample starry-night.jpg or any other image. Stay faithful to the painting's composition and palette (the great spiral and swirling currents of the sky, the haloed stars, the glowing crescent moon, the dark flame-like cypress on the left, the rolling hills, and the village with its church spire), rendered in Van Gogh's thick, directional brushstrokes, and bring it to life: the sky's swirls flow, the stars and moon pulse with light, the cypress sways, and the village windows glow and flicker. Aim for the most impressive result you can make. A helper is provided: run node shot.js --help to see how to screenshot index.html at several moments; look at the screenshots next to the reference and keep improving until you are satisfied, then reply with a short summary of what you made.

We gave Inkling 2 Mini a photo of a hand-drawn Trip Split wireframe and a one-paragraph prompt in the Pi coding harness. Inkling used the sketch’s labels, sample expenses, and handwritten notes to build the expense list, add-expense form, and balances view in a single HTML file with vanilla CSS and JavaScript. The app updates totals and balances when expenses change, suggests payments to settle the trip, and saves data in the browser’s localStorage so it survives a reload.

We ran three independent Inkling attempts and used Playwright to click through each build, checking screenshots where visual judgment was needed. The first attempt, shown here, passed all 13 checks. Adding the sketch’s $90 dinner raised the total from $405 to $495 and recalculated what each person owed.

The photo sketch.jpg in this folder is a product designer's hand-drawn wireframe of a small app. Build that app for real, as the most impressive, original, production-quality version you can make: a single self-contained index.html in this folder using vanilla HTML, CSS and JavaScript only (no frameworks, CDNs, external files or network requests; localStorage is fine), which must run smoothly in desktop Chrome at 1920x1080. Treat everything on the paper as the spec: every screen, label, button and number, the example data, and each red note describe behaviour that must actually work, while the visual design, typography and motion are yours to make beautiful. Look at the sketch carefully with your vision, and use your vision again to check your own work: node shot.cjs --help explains a provided helper that screenshots index.html in headless Chrome at any window size after clicks or other JavaScript steps (Playwright is also installed if you prefer your own scripts), and you can look at any screenshot with the read tool. Click through every feature, compare each screen against the sketch, and keep improving until you are fully satisfied; then reply with a short summary of what you built.

Model is quite autonomous, it has made its own SVGs for the visuals on the website, and even built the matching logic, all from a short prompt: "Can you make a website for my saas called plant therapy where I match house plants with licensed therapists so plants don’t die, return single HTML”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CISA has added one new vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-115731 Perforce Puppet Enterprise Deserialization of Untrusted Data Vulnerability This type of vulnerability is a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and poses significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria. Aware of an exploited vulnerability not at the moment listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

#7426. Introducing managed cluster extensions for observability and user management in Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Slurm

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3557 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Amazon ↗ Open Full Page

Introducing managed cluster extensions for observability and user management in Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Slurm

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3557 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Keeping a shared Slurm cluster for foundation model development in sync entails keeping several separately maintained pieces of configuration matched to what’s running on the nodes.
  • We believe cluster configurations should be managed the way you manage the rest of your AWS infrastructure.
  • According to recent reports, in this post, we walk through the features we introduced in 2026 and explain why the software on running nodes needed a different mechanism.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Keeping a shared Slurm cluster for foundation model development in sync entails keeping several separately maintained pieces of configuration matched to what’s running on the nodes. The cluster’s shape lives on multiple configuration files, its software in custom scripts, its network topology in files that must be edited as nodes change, and its users in a roster that an administrator must maintain and rerun. Over time these pieces drift away from what’s actually running, and nothing tells you when they do.

We believe cluster configurations should be managed the way you manage the rest of your AWS infrastructure. You declare what you want through an API or the console, AWS validates it before it’s applied, the cluster is kept in that state continuously, and you can see whether it’s working. During 2026, Amazon SageMaker HyperPod brought that approach to Slurm clusters, with API-driven Slurm configuration, AMI-based configuration, continuous provisioning, automatic topology management, and deep health checks. Today, we launched cluster extensions, which bring the same approach to the software and settings on running nodes, with managed extensions for observability and user management. However, through all of it, you still keep full access to every node in your cluster, including the controller node. You can SSH in, configure nodes directly, and run your own lifecycle scripts. The APIs give you less to maintain, direct access gives you more control, and you choose the balance.

According to recent reports, in this post, we walk through the features we introduced in 2026 and explain why the software on running nodes needed a different mechanism. We then show how cluster extensions work, through both the API and the console, and follow a platform team through a quarter on a cluster that uses them.

In a recent development, we can think of a Slurm cluster’s configuration grouped into six layers. Five of them describe the cluster itself: its definition, node setup, capacity, network topology, and hardware health. The sixth covers the software running on its nodes, which we discuss in the next section. The following figure shows the six layers.

Earlier in 2026, we brought declarative management to the first five layers. With API-driven Slurm configuration, administrators define node roles, partitions, and Amazon FSx for Lustre and Amazon FSx for OpenZFS mounts in CreateCluster and UpdateCluster requests, and connect an external accounting database. HyperPod updates partition settings while preserving other controller-node Slurm customizations. AMI-based configuration replaces routine setup scripts with images preconfigured with Slurm, Docker, Enroot, Pyxis, and home directories. A custom AMI or OnInitComplete script handles organization-specific software. Continuous provisioning for Slurm retries capacity requests in the background; AMI-based configuration works with it, minimum capacity requirements let teams specify MinInstanceCount, and cluster operations track scaling requests.

Industry observers note that automatic topology management maintains the network layout as nodes scale or are replaced. On Slurm 25.11 or later, partition-level topology supports tree or block topology per partition. For hardware health, on-demand deep health checks stress GPUs and test NVIDIA Collective Communications Library (NCCL) connectivity, while deep health checks with continuous provisioning run as nodes are provisioned. Nodes under check stay in Slurm maintenance reservations until checks finish, keeping jobs off them.

In a recent development, the five layers described so far are configurations that HyperPod can derive or apply once, when it provisions a node. The sixth layer, the software that runs on the nodes, behaves differently because it keeps changing for the life of the cluster. As researchers join and leave, a team asks for deeper GPU metrics for a week, and an exporter ships a fix. For this layer, lifecycle scripts have been the main mechanism so far, and they have drawbacks when the software keeps changing. A script runs only when a node is provisioned, so each change means editing it and then replacing nodes or rerunning it across the fleet. A mistake indicates only when the script runs on a node, and nothing reports what’s installed, so nodes drift apart over time.

In a recent development, we wanted the software to be declared in one place, checked when you submit it, kept consistent across nodes, and visible afterward. In November 2026, we rolled out cluster extensions, which are software packages managed by AWS that you install, configure, update, and remove through APIs or the Amazon SageMaker AI console, starting with observability and user management, including directory integration, as the first software extensions. Compared with scripts, extensions have these advantages:.

Use cluster extensions when HyperPod offers a managed software capability. Use custom AMIs and lifecycle scripts for organization-specific software or initialization that the available extensions don’t cover. HyperPod supports two cluster managed extensions today:.

The following diagram reveals how an extension reaches your nodes.

Figure 2: HyperPod can install, edit, or remove an extension. HyperPod records the desired configuration, a node agent applies the extension package on every node, including latest and replaced ones, and health probes report status and health complications back.

Recent findings suggest that you can use cluster extensions from the SageMaker AI console or through an API. On the console, the Extensions tab on a cluster’s details page lists each extension with its status, version, and ARN, and it’s where you install a new one. Each extension adds controls of its own, such as the metric store and an open dashboard in Grafana button for observability, and the number of customers and groups and a Manage users button for user management. You can also manage every extension through APIs, from the AWS CLI or an SDK, to script installs, keep settings in version control, repeat a setup across clusters, or check status and health from your own tooling. The following table lists the six cluster extension APIs, from installing an extension to listing the versions you can upgrade to, along with console view for extensions.

It has been revealed that figure 3: Left, the six cluster extension APIs and what each one does. Right, the console view to add and remove extensions.

The following diagram reveals what happens after you call one of these APIs.

It has been revealed that figure 4: You declare an extension’s version and settings through the API. HyperPod validates and records them, applies them to every node for its role, and reports status and health.

Industry observers note that when you create or enhancement an extension, HyperPod validates your settings against the version’s schema during the API call, so a misspelled setting is rejected immediately. It then records the version and settings as the desired state and applies them, with each node installing only what its role needs, such as GPU exporters on GPU nodes only. New and replacement nodes get the same state a few minutes after they start, and every node reports whether the extension applied and whether it’s healthy.

Sources indicate that updates send only the settings that you want to change, and HyperPod merges them into the stored settings. Problems that show up only on a node, such as a port or user ID that something else already uses, appear in the Health field of DescribeClusterExtension, grouped by cause with a code, a message, and a count of affected nodes. HyperPod retries internal failures on its own, and for anything else you fix the cause and call UpdateClusterExtension with no changes to retry the affected nodes.

Industry observers note that an extension’s status is Creating or Updating while a change rolls out, Active when every node runs the requested version and settings and none reports a problem, and Degraded when some nodes failed or report a problem. Each extension has its own ARN, so a platform team can own sagemaker-user-management while a monitoring team owns sagemaker-observability. Each health glitch names the component, describes the effect on your cluster, gives the next step, and counts the affected nodes, so you can see where to look without signing in to each node, as the following figure reveals.

Figure 5: An extension’s status, and an example health issue for a node exporter that isn’t running.

A useful way to decide is to ask who owns the software and how often it changes. Some of the software on a cluster is specific to your organization, such as security agents, license servers, and the storage layout your data pipeline expects. Lifecycle scripts and custom AMIs are the right tools for it, because only your team knows what it needs. The rest is software that almost every cluster needs, like GPU and job metrics and user accounts with consistent IDs and access rules. That software must match on every node and keeps changing, so cluster extensions are the better fit, because you declare it once, HyperPod validates it, and each extension reports whether it’s healthy.

The two approaches can coexist, but each component should have one owner. Don’t manage the same exporter, user, or service through both a lifecycle script and an extension, because competing configurations can cause installation or runtime conflicts. Cluster extensions work with every lifecycle configuration option.

Industry observers note that if you already run these capabilities from scripts, you can move to extensions one capability at a time, and scripts and extensions can run side by side while you do. For each capability, the migration takes four steps:.

Sources indicate that if anything is left behind, the install names the conflict, such as a port that’s already in use, and DescribeClusterExtension shows it under Health. With user management, you keep the same usernames and user IDs. The following figure shows four steps.

Figure 6: Moving an existing cluster from lifecycle scripts to extensions, one capability at a time.

You need a HyperPod Slurm cluster on or after the November 2, 2026 HyperPod AMI or later with continuous provisioning enabled. An extension runs software as root on every node, so treat CreateClusterExtension, UpdateClusterExtension, and DeleteClusterExtension as administrator permissions. We suggest that you do not grant them to the cluster’s execution role, because every user who can sign in to the nodes can use its credentials. That role does need access to the destinations that the extensions use, which means Amazon CloudWatch or aps:RemoteWrite for observability and secretsmanager:GetSecretValue for the Active Directory secrets that user management reads. If those secrets are encrypted with a customer managed AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) key, the role also needs kms:Decrypt on that key. User management also needs a shared file system, such as Amazon FSx for Lustre, for home directories.

For procedures, IAM policies, and configuration references, see Cluster extensions for Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Slurm clusters in the Amazon SageMaker AI Developer Guide.

Recent findings suggest that to see how cluster extensions are used in practice, consider a platform team that manages a shared Slurm cluster for several research groups. The team needs a reviewable cluster definition, GPU and job metrics, corporate directory access, local accounts for a partner lab, and separate ownership of observability and user management. The following examples show how the team configures these capabilities and responds to routine changes and failures.

The administrator declares the whole cluster, including node roles, partitions, FSx mounts, minimum capacity, deep health checks, and the external accounting database, in a single CreateCluster request. For a complete example request, see Getting started with SageMaker HyperPod using the AWS CLI.

The request has no lifecycle configuration, topology file, or Slurm configuration file. Each SlurmConfig gives its instance group a role, and the GPU group joins the train partition. AMI-based configuration sets up the nodes, and the security team’s compliance agent is already in the custom AMI. The GPU group asks for 8 nodes and requires 6, so jobs can start as soon as 6 are ready while HyperPod provisions the rest and health checks each GPU node as it arrives. HyperPod selects tree topology for the P5 nodes on its own, and accounting writes to an Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) database that the team owns. The administrator can still SSH into the controller node to inspect or tune Slurm directly.

It has been revealed that leadership wants GPU and job metrics, so the administrator installs the observability extension. In the SageMaker AI console, on the cluster’s Extensions tab, the administrator chooses the observability extension, picks the metric categories and their levels and the collection interval, and selects one of two metric stores: Amazon CloudWatch or Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus. The following screenshot demonstrates the install form with one store selected. The other option is available in the same field.

Figure 7: Installing the observability extension from the console, with configurable metric levels and a choice of metric store.

According to recent reports, the same installation through the API takes one create-cluster-extension call. The following example uses Amazon CloudWatch as the metric store. To send metrics to Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus instead, you set the Prometheus destination in the same configuration.

The administrator installs the extension with one create-cluster-extension call:.

The call returns the extension’s ARN, which the administrator uses in later calls:.

Recent findings suggest that whichever way it’s installed, each node runs only the components relevant to its role, such as DCGM and EFA exporters on GPU nodes and Slurm cluster metrics on the controller. Schema errors are rejected before rollout, while node-specific conflicts appear in extension health.

In a recent development, after the install, the extension appears on the cluster’s Extensions tab with its version, status, and ARN. The screenshot reveals the tab for a cluster that has both the observability and user management extensions installed, and both are Active.

Figure 8: The Extensions tab for a cluster with both the observability and user management extensions installed.

It has been revealed that whichever metric store you choose, you can add an Amazon Managed Grafana workspace to the installation, so the team doesn’t need to build dashboards from scratch. After signing in to Grafana, they find two pre-created dashboards, Clusters and Jobs, as shown in the following screenshot.

Figure 9: The Clusters and Jobs dashboards that come with the observability extension in Amazon Managed Grafana.

It has been revealed that the Clusters dashboard gives a single view of your HyperPod Slurm clusters, built on the metrics that the extension collects and sends to your chosen metric store. At the top, it summarizes cluster health: instance count and health, GPU and GPU memory totals, vCPUs, memory, and Amazon FSx for Lustre capacity. It also indicates the state of Slurm itself, including node states (idle, allocated, mixed, down, and draining), job queues, failed or preempted jobs, and scheduler activity. From there, you can filter by cluster, node, or GPU to drill into EFA networking, GPU performance and errors, and host-level CPU, memory, disk, and network metrics, as shown in the following screenshots. That lets you go from “is my cluster healthy?” to the root cause of an glitch without leaving the dashboard.

Figure 10: The Clusters dashboard, from cluster-wide health and Slurm state down to per-node GPU, EFA, and host metrics.

Sources indicate that the Jobs dashboard moves from cluster-level health down to individual Slurm jobs. It ties each job’s resource to use back to the job itself, using metrics from the Slurm job exporter in either metric store. You can filter by cluster, job ID, job name, partition, user, or account, and see CPU, memory, GPU utilization, GPU memory, and disk I/O for each job, plus accelerator and NCCL metrics. That makes it easier to spot underused GPUs, stuck jobs, or communication bottlenecks in distributed training, as in the following screenshot.

Figure 11: The Jobs dashboard, showing resource use for individual Slurm jobs.

Later, a research team that is tuning multi-node training asks for more detail, so the administrator sends only the settings to change:.

HyperPod merges these settings into the stored configuration and applies them to every node, restarting only the components whose settings changed. When the investigation is over, setting both to null returns them to their defaults, and at no point are nodes replaced or scripts rerun.

In a recent development, one morning the extension shows as Degraded. A newly introduced instance group has an execution role that lacks aps:RemoteWrite, and describe-cluster-extension shows the effect:.

Once the administrator adds the permission, the nodes report healthy and the extension returns to Active, with nothing to reinstall.

Sources indicate that the user management extension manages the Linux users and groups on every node, and who can sign in and use sudo on each node type. You declare who should exist and what they can do, and HyperPod applies it to every node, including nodes added later or replaced, so no one connects to nodes or runs scripts to add or remove a user. Users come from local accounts that you list in the configuration, from Active Directory over LDAPS, or from both, and each group names the node types (controller, login, or compute) where its members can sign in over SSH and where they get passwordless sudo.

Recent findings suggest that for the platform team, security wants corporate identities, with sudo reserved for administrators, and a partner lab that isn’t in the directory needs accounts of its own. The administrator declares both sources in one configuration, with group rules that say which node types each group can sign in to and use sudo on:.

Access is explicit, so after the extension is installed only the groups that grant SSH access, along with the default ubuntu user, can sign in. Directory consumers keep their identities and group membership in Active Directory, while the partner lab’s users get the same IDs, home directories, and the default Slurm root account.

In a recent development, the same configuration can be managed from the console. Choosing Manage users on the user management extension opens the cluster’s Users tab, where the administrator can add, edit, and remove groups and users, and set which node types each group can sign in to and use sudo on, as shown in the following screenshot.

Figure 12: Managing groups and consumers for the user management extension on the console.

When AWS publishes a latest version of an extension, the administrator lists the versions that can be installed and upgrades in place without AMI updates:.

In a recent development, hyperPod checks the stored settings against the upcoming version’s schema and rejects the request, changing nothing, if they aren’t valid for it. Otherwise, the new version rolls out to every node, and nodes that join later get it too. Upgrades only go forward, so the administrator picks a maintenance window. Any new settings or capabilities that come with the version can then be turned on with an update like the earlier one.

Before the end-of-quarter run, the administrator starts an on-demand deep health check on the GPU group and then adds nodes with batch-add-cluster-nodes. The request returns as soon as HyperPod accepts it, so the administrator follows it as a cluster operation:.

As capacity arrives, each node is health checked, joins Slurm, takes its place in the topology, and gets both extensions with the same version and settings as every other node. If a GPU fails during the run, the replacement is configured and picks up the extensions the same way.

At the end of the quarter, security asks who has sudo on the controller, and the administrator answers from the API without signing in to a node:.

Recent findings suggest that the answer is cluster-admins and ClusterAdmin@example.com, and the directory group’s membership is audited in the directory. Because each extension has its own ARN, the platform team’s role can patch only sagemaker-user-management and the monitoring team’s role only sagemaker-observability, while security has read-only access to both. None of these permissions belongs on the cluster’s execution role. When an extension is Active, ActiveCount equals TotalCount, and Health is empty, every node runs exactly that configuration.

Cluster extensions, including the observability and user management extensions, have been available since November 2026 in all the regions where Amazon SageMaker HyperPod is supported, and the other improvements in this post were announced earlier in 2026, with each announcement listing its Regions. There’s no additional charge for cluster extensions. You pay for the AWS resources that you use with them, such as Amazon CloudWatch, Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus, and AWS Secrets Manager.

Figure 13: The two extensions that have been available since November 2026.

A cluster is easier to run when more of it is declared, validated, converged, and observable. This year’s improvements brought that to a HyperPod Slurm cluster’s definition, node setup, capacity, network topology, and hardware health, and cluster extensions, available since November 2026, bring it to the software on the nodes, the layer that changes most often. Lifecycle scripts and custom AMIs stay focused on what’s specific to your organization, and the controller node stays yours.

To create a cluster as described in this post, see Getting started with SageMaker HyperPod using the AWS CLI. To get started with cluster extensions, see Cluster Extensions in the Amazon SageMaker AI Developer Guide. Share your feedback in the comments or through your AWS account team.

Recent findings suggest that this feature has contributions across several teams. Some of the people involved in developing this include Hengyu Lou, Aman Pratap Singh, Karthick Ravi, Shubh Nisar, Nitish Sai Kommasai, Uday Singamala, Min Badar, Devanshi Desai, Yahya Hassan, Connie Chen, Kashish Tayal, Oleg Talalov, Takuma Yoshitami, Kiran Penta, Dhawal Parkar, Pradeep Cruz.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Purpose CISA strongly urges organizations to immediately patch the recently disclosed Oracle Java vulnerability CVE-2026-114938. This critical memory-corruption vulnerability, known as “Java4Shell,” affects the Base64 decoder of the x86-64 HotSpot Java Virtual Machine (JVM), which is part of the Java Development Kit (JDK). Specially crafted Base64 input could crash the JVM and allow for unauthenticated remote code execution. Actions to take CISA urges organizations to take the following actions: Identify affected Java installations. Review your software inventory for JDKs and Java runtimes, including those bundled with third-party applications or included in container images and appliances. Note: JDKs and Java runtimes may not appear as separate entries in software inventories. Apply relevant Java and vendor patches as soon as they are available, prioritizing internet-facing systems. If immediate patching is not feasible, implement temporary compensating controls, such as restricting and validating Base64 input at the application boundary, enforcing input-size limits, and limiting unauthenticated access. Review Oracle’s security advisory for guidance on patching and affected products and versions. Monitor for indicators of suspicious activity, including rogue runtimes, unexpected JVM crashes, and suspicious Java processes. Resources CISA urges network defenders to review the following resource and apply necessary updates: Vendor Guidance Oracle’s Security Advisory: Critical Security Patch Revision – November 2026 Disclaimer The information in this report is being provided “as is” for informational purposes only.
